sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text:
Vibration-based energy harvesters have been developed as power sources for wireless sensor networks. Because the vibration frequency of the environment is varied with surrounding conditions, how to design an adaptive energy harvester is a practical topic. This paper proposes a design for a piezoelectric energy harvester possessing the ability to self-adjust its resonant frequency in rotational environments. The effective length of a trapezoidal cantilever is extended by centrifugal force from a rotating wheel to vary its area moment of inertia. The analytical solution for the natural frequency of the piezoelectric energy harvester was derived from the parameter design process, which could specify a structure approaching resonance at any wheel rotating frequency. The kinetic equation and electrical damping induced by power generation were derived from a Lagrange method and a mechanical–electrical coupling model, respectively. An energy harvester with adequate parameters can generate power at a wide range of car speeds. The output power of an experimental prototype composed of piezoelectric thin films and connected to a $3 . 3 { \mathrm { M } } \Omega$ external resistor was approximately $7 0 { - } 1 4 0 \mu \mathrm { W }$ at wheel speeds ranging from 200 to $7 0 0 ~ \mathrm { R P M }$ . These results demonstrate that the proposed piezoelectric energy harvester can be applied as a power source for the wireless tire pressure monitoring sensor.

Keywords: natural frequency, self-tuning, piezoelectric cantilever, wheel (Some figures may appear in colour only in the online journal)

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
With the rapid development of the automobile industry, carmakers are highly motivated to improve automotive safety for drivers. According to the data from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, a tire $2 5 \%$ below its recommended pressure is three times more likely to be involved in a crash than a tire at its recommended pressure. A tire pressure monitoring system (TPMS) provides real-time tire pressure and temperature detection during driving. If the tire pressure is abnormal, TPMS immediately warns the driver to avoid the possibility of an accident. Existing TPMSs are installed in automobile wheels and are powered by batteries; however, battery-powered tire pressure sensors have notable disadvantages. Because batteries have a finite lifespan, they require replacement, which can be inconvenient; the exhausted batteries might pollute the environment. Therefore, in the literature, the effective harvesting of kinetic energy from rotating wheels to power TPMSs is discussed frequently.

Various methods have been proposed to convert kinetic energy into electrical energy, including piezoelectricity [1–13], electromagnetic induction [14–18], and electrostatics [19]. A previous study proposed a piezoelectric energy harvester for rotary motion [2]. The harvester could convert a maximum power of $6 . 4 \mathrm { m W }$ when the structure resonated at a rotational speed of $1 3 8 \mathrm { r a d s } ^ { - 1 }$ , but the power decreased dramatically for structures that fell out of resonance. To increase the operating frequency range of energy harvesters, researchers have established strategies including active and passive adjusting methods to tune the natural frequencies of energy harvesters. Several active adjusting methods have been proposed, such as using piezoelectric actuators to change the geometry [3]; moving the center of gravity of proof mass [4]; and applying axial force to tune the resonant frequency [5]. Although these methods can actively adjust the resonant frequency of energy harvesters, they consume extra power during the adjusting process. Therefore, some passive adjusting methods have been proposed, and most studies have used nonlinear elements for harvesting energy in a broad frequency range. One study proposed an offset pendulum energy harvester for rotational environments; this harvester used a nonlinear bistable restoring spring to improve the operating frequency range of the system [6]. Another noncontact piezoelectric energy harvester used a nonlinear magnetic levitation structure to widen its operating frequency range [7]. An alternative nonlinear broadband piezoelectric energy harvester with rotatable magnets was presented [8], the overall wide bandwidth of $4 { - } 2 2 \mathrm { H z }$ was obtained by adjusting the magnet inclination angle. Zhang et al [9] proposed a bistable energy harvester to scavenge energy from rotational environments. With theoretical model, the harvester can be optimized by application of stochastic resonance. Wu et al [10] proposed a seesaw-structured energy harvester that could weaken the influence of centrifugal force. A pendulum-driven passive self-adjusting energy harvester was proposed [11]; the natural frequency of the pendulum depended on the centrifugal force caused by wheel rotation, and it almost matched the driving frequency at an intersection frequency of $1 5 \mathrm { H z }$ . Niri and Salamone proposed a passively tunable energy harvester that used a sliding mechanism to adjust the stiffness and axial load [12]. A suitably weighted pendulum was presented to harvest vibration energy from a rotating wheel [15, 16]; the adequate design enabled the system to tune its natural frequency to coincide with the rotation frequency. In contrast to the proposed device in this paper, the energy harvesters [15, 16] consumed the kinetic energy due to the friction of the revolving joints particularly at high wheel speeds. That is because the centrifugal force varies with the square of the wheel speed. A device with a magnetoelectric transducer was proposed [17]; this device used axial tensile stress caused by centrifugal force to tune its natural frequency; two magnets located beside the tip mass enhanced the deflection angle.

An energy harvester embedded in the inner surface of the tire was proposed [18], which differed from rim-mounted energy harvesters. When a mounted device hits or leaves the ground, a drastic impact force is applied to the energy harvester. The output power increases with the rotation speed. Several adequately designed piezoelectric energy harvesters have been made with compact structures and have provided high output voltages [20, 21]. This paper proposes a piezoelectric energy harvester with a trapezoidal cantilever mounted on the rim, and the area moment of inertia of the cantilever can be self-adjusted by centrifugal force to tune its natural frequency for harvesting various quantities of kinetic energy in a wide range of wheel rotation speeds.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In section 2, the kinetic model of the trapezoidal cantilever is derived using the Euler–Lagrange method and the Bernoulli– Euler beam theory. In section 3, the parameters are calculated for the resonance in a wide range of wheel rotation speeds. In section 4, the dynamic behavior is calculated using numerical simulation; the different weighted block locations that affect the deflection angles and power generation are presented. In section 5, electrical damping induced by the current delivered to an electrical load is established. The simulations are compared with the experimental results and some conclusions are offered in sections 6 and 7, respectively.

sections.heading: 2. Kinetic equation of the energy harvester

Consider a cantilever with a weighted block mounted on a rotating wheel, as shown in figure 1. The outer radius of the car wheel is $R _ { 1 }$ , and the distance between the end of the cantilever and the wheel center is $R _ { 2 }$ . The cantilever with the I-shaped weighted block is assembled in a foundation mounted on the wheel ring.

sections.heading: 3. Configuration and parameter design
sections.text: The structure of the energy harvester is shown in figure 2(a). We designed a trapezoidal cantilever that consisted of a rubber plate, as shown in figure 2(b). We used a tension spring to connect the cantilever and the foundation. Four roller bearings were mounted on the foundation to clamp the extendable cantilever, and an I-shaped weighted block was attached to the cantilever. A steel wire attached the I-shaped weighted block to the foundation, allowing the weighted block to swing with respect to the cantilever root at a constant distance $a$ . Four polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) films were attached to the bottom surface of the cantilever in parallel to transfer electrical power. The PVDF films used in this study were manufactured by Mouser Specialties Inc., Model No. $\mathrm { D T } 2 – 0 2 8 \mathrm { K L } ^ { - 1 }$ . The substrate of the proposed cantilever was made of polysiloxanes. When the wheel rotates, the I-shaped weighted block applies an alteration force on the cantilever. The effective length of the trapezoidal cantilever is extended by centrifugal force; hence, the area moment of inertia at the root of the trapezoidal cantilever varies to adjust its natural frequency. With adequate parameters, the radical term in equation (18) approaches unity; thus, the trapezoidal cantilever resonates at any wheel rotation speed. The variation of $I _ { \mathrm { t } }$ is small for different car speeds because the mass moment of inertia of the I-shaped weighted block is much larger than that of the trapezoidal cantilever. Therefore, $\gamma$ is almost invariant with $\dot { \Theta }$ . Furthermore, $R _ { 2 }$ is decided by the geometry of the wheel rim; $m _ { 2 }$ and $a$ are two design parameters that maintain $\gamma$ at a value less than 1. The denominator of $\lambda$ is proportional to $\dot { \Theta } ^ { 2 }$ . For a trapezoidal cantilever, $\beta$ and $L$ are known to exist and $L$ is a function of $\dot { \Theta } ^ { 2 }$ . With adequate parameters, $\lambda$ can be invariant with $\dot { \Theta }$ . If the cantilever is rectangular $\beta = 0$ ,) then $\lambda$ decreases with the car speed.

sections.heading: 4. Dynamic analysis
sections.text:
This section discusses the dynamic behavior of the cantilever by solving equation (15). The dynamic behavior can be determined by two independent parameters: weighted distance a and the generalized damping constant $C _ { T }$ , when the dimensions of the wheel and the velocity and acceleration of the car are known. The geometric parameters of the proposed energy harvester are listed in table 1 and the characteristics of the PVDF with regard to output power are listed in table 2. In numerical studies, $C _ { T }$ was $\bar { 0 . 5 5 \ \mathrm { N - s } } \mathrm { k g } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { m } ^ { - 1 }$ , as shown in figures 3–7. Figure 3 shows the time domain response of the deflection angle at $6 0 \mathrm { k m h } ^ { - 1 }$ ; the deflection angle became steady after $1 5 \mathrm { s }$ , and the maximum deflection angle was approximately $7 6 ^ { \circ }$ . The vibration frequency corresponded to the wheel rotation frequency. To verify the effects of weighted block locations, the frequency ratio $\omega _ { n } / \dot { \Theta }$ at various car speeds with different weighted block locations were simulated, as illustrated in figure 4. The curve $a = ~ 3 . 9 \mathrm { m m }$ was closest to $\omega _ { n } / \dot { \Theta } = 1$ for car speeds ranging from 30 to $1 4 0 \mathrm { k m h } ^ { - 1 }$ . Given an adequate weighted block location of the I-shaped weighted block and given the self-adjustability of area moment of inertia, the natural frequency of the trapezoidal cantilever varies with the car speed and approaches the wheel rotation frequency in a range of car speed. At low wheel rotation speeds (i.e., under $2 5 \mathrm { k m h } ^ { - 1 } ,$ ), the frequency ratio was large, because the small $\dot { \Theta }$ caused the denominator of $\lambda$ to become small. Variations of the power density versus car speed with different weighted block locations. Figure 5 displays the variations of the deflection angle of the piezoelectric cantilever versus car speed. For designs in which $a = 3 . 7$ and $3 . 8 \mathrm { m m }$ , the deflection angle behaved a peak value at resonant frequency corresponding to $\omega _ { n } / \dot { \Theta } = 1$ in figure 4. For designs in which $a = 4 . 0$ and $4 . 1 \mathrm { m m }$ , the deflection angle monotonically decreased with car speed, because the frequency ratio never approached unity for the simulated car speeds. The maximum angular velocity $\dot { \theta }$ of the cantilever varied with the car speed at different weighted block locations as shown in figure 6. For the design in which $a = 3 . 9 \mathrm { m m }$ , the deflection angle came the closest to $\omega _ { n } / \dot { \Theta } = 1$ , and this design had the widest frequency range for the angular velocity. This result proves that the adequate weighted block location and the natural frequency selfadjusting mechanism enhance the kinetic energy of the wheelrim-mounted cantilever. Although the damping caused the natural frequency to differ from the resonant frequency, the difference was nonsignificant. The harvested power is proportional to the square of the angular velocity of the cantilever. We define a power density as the steady-state maximum output power in a period per mass moment of inertia of an energy harvester $( C _ { T } \dot { \theta } _ { \operatorname* { m a x } } ^ { 2 } \big / I _ { t } )$ to compare the performance for different designs. In the swing motion, the mass moment of inertia is more representative than the mass. The power density versus car speed with different weighted block locations is shown in figure 7. This estimate assumes that the energy transformation occurs without loss $\varphi _ { T } = C _ { e } ,$ . For designs in which $a \geqslant 4 . 0 \mathrm { m m }$ , the small power was due to the fact that the frequency ratio was not close to unity at any simulated car speed. For designs in which $a \leqslant 3 . 8 \mathrm { m m }$ , resonance occurred at low car speeds, and the produced power immediately dropped when the wheel rotation frequency increased away the resonant frequency. ![](images/76160b85b49ba7f0f2a2500a43dc8e37d4f24100ae97dbbda0ca3428a123bf10.jpg) Figure 8. Variations of the power density versus car speed with different dampings. Figure 8 shows the variations of the steady-state maximum power per inertia versus car speed with different damping constants for the design in which $a = 3 . 9 \mathrm { m m }$ . For large damping constants, the frequency range of the output power was wide, but its peak value was small. The opposite holds true for small damping constants. A damping constant for the energy harvester involves a tradeoff between a wide frequency range and a large output power. The electrical damping constant of the piezoelectric energy harvester varies with its strain rate, depends on the related material properties, and is not a constant value. The electrical damping is calculated based on the mechanical–electrical coupling model described in the next section.

sections.heading: 5. Mechanical–electrical coupling model
sections.text:
A resistive load is applied to deliver the power to a real electrical load. According to the model of the piezoelectric equivalent circuit, the output voltage of the piezoelectric cantilever connected to an external resistive load is related to the strain rate as [11]

$$
\begin{array} { r } { V = R C _ { b } \frac { 2 t _ { c } d _ { 3 1 } E _ { p } } { a \varepsilon } \dot { S } - R C _ { b } \dot { V } , } \end{array}
$$

where $R$ is the external load receiving the electrical energy; $C _ { b } = { a _ { 1 } } ^ { 2 } \varepsilon B L / 2 t _ { c }$ is the capacitance; $s$ is the average strain; and $a _ { 1 } , t _ { c } , d _ { 3 1 } , \varepsilon$ , and $E _ { p }$ are the series or parallel coefficient, thickness, piezoelectric strain coefficient, dielectric constant, and Young’s modulus of the PVDF, respectively. In a parallel connection, $a _ { 1 }$ is 2. The average strain of a cantilever with a weighted block is

$$
\begin{array} { r } { S = \frac { \sigma } { E } = \frac { M c } { E I } = \frac { m _ { 2 } a c } { 2 E I } , } \end{array}
$$

where $\sigma$ is the average stress of the cantilever, $M$ is the moment caused by the I-shaped weighted block, and $c = h / 2$ . According to the Euler–Bernoulli beam theory, the deflection angle at the position at which the weighted block is placed is

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \theta = \frac { m _ { 2 } a ^ { 2 } } { 2 E I } . } \end{array}
$$

Substituting equation (21) into equation (20), strain can be written as

$$
\begin{array} { r } { S = \frac { c } { a } \theta . } \end{array}
$$

The piezoelectric films are considered as transducers that transform kinetic energy into electrical energy. According to the law of conservation of energy, electrical energy must equal mechanical energy; thus, power is written as follows:

$$
\begin{array} { r } { P = \frac { V ^ { 2 } } { R } = C _ { E } \cdot \Big ( \frac { d \theta } { d t } \Big ) ^ { 2 } . } \end{array}
$$

To make the operation easier, $\dot { S }$ and $\dot { V }$ are rewritten as

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \dot { S } = \frac { \mathrm { d } S } { \mathrm { d } t } = \frac { \mathrm { d } S } { \mathrm { d } \theta } \cdot \frac { \mathrm { d } \theta } { \mathrm { d } t } , } \\ { \dot { V } = \frac { \mathrm { d } V } { \mathrm { d } t } = \frac { \mathrm { d } V } { \mathrm { d } \theta } \cdot \frac { \mathrm { d } \theta } { \mathrm { d } t } . } \end{array}
$$

Substituting equations (19)–(22) and (24) and (25) into equation (23), the electrical damping is obtained as

$$
\begin{array} { r } { C _ { E } = R \bigg ( { a _ { 1 1 } } ^ { 2 } \Big ( \frac { c } { a } \Big ) ^ { 2 } + { C _ { b } } ^ { 2 } \Big ( \frac { \dot { V } } { \dot { \theta } } \Big ) ^ { 2 } - 2 a _ { 1 1 } { C _ { b } } \frac { c } { a } \cdot \frac { \dot { V } } { \dot { \theta } } \bigg ) , } \end{array}
$$

where $a _ { 1 1 } = a _ { 1 } B L d _ { 3 1 } E _ { p }$ . By substituting equation (26) into (15) and solving equations (15) and (19) simultaneously, the two unknowns of output voltage and deflection angle are obtained.

sections.heading: 6. Simulations and experiments for power generation
sections.text:
Simulations considering the mechanical–electrical coupling are shown in figures 9 and 10 for $a = 3 . 9 \mathrm { m m }$ . The horizontal axis represents both equivalent car speed and plate rotational speed because the experiment was performed on a rotatable plate. The kinetic effect provided by the rotatable plate is the same with that by the rolling wheel at constant angular speed. The output voltage increased with the external load, but the voltage reached a saturation value at $1 0 0 \mathbf { M } \boldsymbol { \Omega }$ external load. The output voltage decreased with the car speed due to the decreased angular velocity of the cantilever at high car speeds. The mechanical damping value was estimated from the free vibration experiment without the external load. The output power shown in figure 10 was estimated from the square of output voltage divided by the external load resistance. A large external resistance, e.g. 100 and $1 5 0 \mathbf { M } \Omega$ , did not correspond to a large output power. An optimum external resistance exists for a given constant car speed, and that resistance produces maximum output power based on impedance matching. A low external resistance, e.g. $3 . 3 { \mathrm { M } } \Omega$ , induced large electrical damping that produced a wide frequency range for different car speeds, as shown in figure 10.

![](images/bcd16199322d7870925b57a0226d20c1b06fa2f8c004db0a9968c079011c2439.jpg)

Therefore, the $3 . 3 { \mathrm { M } } \Omega$ external load is adopted in the experiment. Moreover, the optimum resistance for the piezoelectric energy harvester corresponding a given rotating speed has been analyzed in prior research [22].

The prototype of energy harvester was mounted on a rotatable plate to measure the output voltage as harvesting the energy from a car wheel rotating at constant speeds. The output voltage was measured using an oscilloscope through a slip ring at the center of the rotatable plate. The prototype shown in the top-left corner of figure 11 was manufactured according to parameters listed in table 1. Figure 12 shows experimental and simulated output voltage and power values of the energy harvester connected to a $3 . 3 { \mathrm { M } } \Omega$ external load. The difference between the simulated and experimental results for output power was larger than that for voltage, because power was proportional to the square of voltage. The experimental output voltage varied with car speed from 10 to

$9 0  { \mathrm { k m h } ^ { - 1 } }$ , which was consistent with the simulated results. Such consistency between the simulated and experimental results verifies the correctness of the kinetic model and the ability of the self-adjusting resonant frequency. We observed that the extension of the trapezoidal cantilever was slightly hindered by the friction force between the cantilever and roller bearings. Moreover, the position of the I-shaped weighted block shifted because of large centrifugal forces. Thus, conducting experiments with high plate rotational speeds (e.g., higher than $1 0 0 \mathrm { k m h } ^ { - 1 }$ ) would be difficult.

sections.heading: 7. Conclusion
sections.text: This paper proposes a novel design for a piezoelectric energy harvester with a trapezoidal cantilever to be used in rotational environments. From the kinetic equation, we found the location at which a weighted block should be fixed relative to the cantilever and the area moment of inertia at the root of the trapezoidal cantilever should be adjusted by centrifugal force to ensure that the natural frequency coincides with the wheel rotation frequency. The numerical results showed that adequate design parameters can effectively increase the output power and widen the frequency range because adequate design parameters enable the system to approach resonance at any wheel rotation frequency. The location of the weighted block is crucial. The trapezoidal cantilever with four PVDF films in parallel can transform mechanical energy to electrical energy. The formulation of electrical damping was derived based on the strain variation of the piezoelectric cantilever and the law of conservation of energy. The external load can be designed to change the value of the electrical damping for different power output profiles at various car speeds. A prototype with a $2 4 \mathrm { - g }$ I-shaped weighted block was manufactured to verify the behavior of the energy harvester. The experimental results indicated that the average power was $1 0 7 . 4 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ for wheel rotation speeds ranging from 177 to 796 RPM. These rotation speeds corresponded to constant car speeds ranging from 20 to $9 0 \mathrm { k m h } ^ { - 1 }$ . For a radio transceiver consuming $8 \mathrm { m W }$ when transmitting could be powered at a duty ratio of $1 . 3 4 \%$ by the proposed energy harvester. This performance demonstrates that the piezoelectric energy harvester has the potential to be a power source for a TPMS that has the average power demand of $2 5 \mu \mathrm { W }$ . The power storage circuit and capacitor will be considered in future studies.
